data.question_title: If \( \left| z _ { 1 } \right| = \left| z _ { 2 } \right| \) and \( \arg \left( \cfrac { z _ { 1 } } { z _ { 2 } } \right) = \pi \) , then \( z _ { 1 } + z _ { 2 } \) is:
data.explanation_txt:
We have \( \arg \left( \cfrac { z _ { 1 } } { z _ { 2 } } \right) = \pi \)

\( \Rightarrow \arg \left( z _ { 1 } \right) - \arg \left( z _ { 2 } \right) = \pi \Rightarrow \arg \left( z _ { 1 } \right) = \arg \left( z _ { 2 } \right) + \pi \)

Let \(\arg \left( z _ { 2 } \right) = \theta\), then \(\arg \left( z _ { 1 } \right) = \pi + \theta\)

\( \therefore z _ { 1 } = | z _ { 1 } | [ \cos ( \pi + \theta ) + i \sin ( \pi + \theta ) ] = |z_1| (-\cos \theta - i \sin \theta ) \)

And \( z _ { 2 } = | z _ { 2 } | ( \cos \theta + i \sin \theta ) = |z_1| (\cos \theta + i \sin \theta ) \) \( ( \since |z_1| = |z_2|) \)

Hence \( z_1 + z_2 = 0 \)

Since \( \sin x \) is positive for \( 0 < x < \pi \) and negative for \( \pi < x < 2\pi \)

\[ |\sin x| = \left \{ \begin{matrix} \sin x & 0 < x < \pi \\ -\sin x & \pi < x < 2 \pi \end{matrix} \right. \]

So, the given integral becomes:

\[ \begin{align} \int _{0}^{\pi }2\sin x\, dx+\int _{\pi }^{2\pi }0.\, dx & =2\, [-\cos x]_{0}^{\pi } +0 \\ & =-2\, (\cos \pi -\cos 0) \\ & =-2\, (-1-1) \\ & =4.\end{align} \]

data.question_title:
When the esteemed Greek philosopher, Eudemos, became seriously ill with a fever, the most famous physician of Rome tried every remedy but to no avail. Death was knocking at his door when Eudemos called in Galen, a young Greek physician who had recently arrived in the city.

The Roman doctors attending Eudemos scoffingly asked the new comer: “to what physician’s sect, and regard as slaves those who accept as final, the teachings of Hippocrates or anyone else.” He then proceeded to prescribe remedies that restored this patient to perfect health with a short time.

Galen was born in 130AD in Pergamon, the capital of the Rome province of Asia Minor, famous for its school of sculpture and for its library which rivaled that of Alexandria. Nicon, the father of Galen, was a wealthy farmer who had attained a well-rounded education in mathematics, philosophy, and the natural sciences. Nicon instilled in his son a love for language and literature and trained him in the fundamental of mathematics and the natural sciences. On the farm, the impressionable boy learned many of the secrets of animal and plant life. when he was fourteen years old, Galen was sent by his father to the best teacher in Pergamon. From reading Aristotle received his first lessons in Biology and learned that the biologist must study nature by direct observation.
